stem: A platform team wants to run its Terraform root modules with Infrastructure Manager instead of a self-managed Jenkins pipeline. Each root module has a `backend "gcs"` block that points to a team state bucket. The root modules call child modules in local subdirectories. What must the team change before the first Infrastructure Manager deployment?

options.text: Remove the backend blocks, because Infrastructure Manager stores and manages the state for each deployment.
Merge the child modules into one file, because Infrastructure Manager accepts only a single Terraform file.
Add a service account key to the provider block, because Cloud Build needs credentials to call Google Cloud APIs.
Grant the Infrastructure Manager service agent access to the state bucket, because it reads the backend block.

explanation: Infrastructure Manager requires that a configuration defines no backend blocks. It handles state management itself and keeps a copy of the state file for each deployment and revision. Local child modules are fine: a configuration can have many files and directories if the entry point is a root module. Credentials are not needed in the code, because Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform as the service account that you name.

whyWrong.B: A configuration can consist of multiple files and directories. Only the entry point must be a Terraform root module.
whyWrong.C: Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform with the identity of the service account that you pass to the deployment. Keys add risk and are not needed.
whyWrong.D: Infrastructure Manager does not use your backend block. Backend blocks must not be defined, and Infrastructure Manager manages the state itself.

sources.title: Deployment Manager deprecation
sources.evidence: Familiarize yourself with Terraform's state management (which involves managing state files and potential state locking issues). Infra Manager handles state management automatically.

sources.title: Terraform and Infrastructure Manager
sources.evidence: These configurations can consist of multiple files and directories, but their entrypoint must be a Terraform root module.

sources.title: Configure the service account
sources.evidence: To use Infrastructure Manager to create, update, or delete a deployment, you must use a service account. Infra Manager executes Terraform using the identity of this service account.

stem: Five engineers run Terraform from their laptops against the same production project. Each laptop keeps its own `terraform.tfstate` file. Last week, two engineers applied changes at the same time, and one state file no longer matched the infrastructure. The team wants the Google-recommended fix with the least operational overhead. What should you recommend?

options.text: Commit `terraform.tfstate` to the Git repository, and require a pull request for every change to the state file.
Give each engineer a separate Terraform CLI workspace in the same local directory, so that the changes do not collide.
Keep the state on a shared Compute Engine VM, and require all engineers to run Terraform over SSH on that VM.
Store the state in a Cloud Storage backend with Object Versioning, and give bucket admin permissions only to a few administrators.

explanation: Google recommends the Cloud Storage state backend for Google Cloud customers. The backend uses state locking, so two engineers cannot change the state at the same time. It also keeps sensitive state data out of version control. Object Versioning keeps earlier versions of the state for recovery. Google also recommends admin permissions on the bucket for only a small set of administrators, and only object read and write permissions for the other developers. The backend is a configuration change, so the overhead is low.

whyWrong.A: Git gives no state locking, and state can contain secrets. Google recommends keeping state out of version control and adding state files to .gitignore.
whyWrong.B: Local workspaces still give each laptop its own view and no shared lock. Google recommends using only the default workspace.
whyWrong.C: A shared VM adds a server to patch, back up, and secure, and it forces everyone onto one machine. The Cloud Storage backend gives locking and versioned state with less work.

sources.title: Best practices for security
sources.evidence: For Google Cloud customers, we recommend using the Cloud Storage state backend. This approach locks the state to allow for collaboration as a team.

sources.title: Store Terraform state in a Cloud Storage bucket
sources.evidence: versioning is enabled to ensure that earlier versions of the state are preserved in the bucket.

sources.title: Store Terraform state in a Cloud Storage bucket
sources.evidence: Only a small set of users (for example, the main cloud administrator and the person acting as the alternative or backup administrator) should have admin permissions for the bucket.

stem: A team manages project IAM with one `google_project_iam_policy` resource that lists the roles for the team's groups. After an apply, Dataflow jobs and GKE node pools in the project fail with permission errors for Google-managed service accounts. The team wants to keep managing its own grants with Terraform. What should the team do?

options.text: Replace the resource with `google_project_iam_binding` resources, one for each role that the team grants.
Replace the resource with `google_project_iam_member` resources, or use Google's IAM module for the grants.
Keep the resource, and add a `lifecycle` block with `prevent_destroy` so that Terraform cannot remove roles.
Keep the resource, and run `terraform refresh` before each apply so that the state includes the new roles.

explanation: `google_*_iam_policy` and `google_*_iam_binding` resources are authoritative. On each run, Terraform overwrites the permissions to match the configuration, which removes roles that Google Cloud manages for its service agents. Google recommends `google_*_iam_member` resources or Google's IAM module. These resources add each grant without removing grants that other systems made.

whyWrong.A: `google_project_iam_binding` is also authoritative. For each role that it manages, it removes members that Terraform does not list.
whyWrong.C: `prevent_destroy` blocks the destruction of the resource itself. It does not stop Terraform from overwriting the policy on an update.
whyWrong.D: A refresh updates the state, but the configuration stays the source of truth. The next apply still removes the roles that the configuration does not list.

sources.title: Best practices when working with Google Cloud resources
sources.evidence: To prevent this, we recommend using either google_*_iam_member resources directly or the IAM module from Google.

sources.title: Best practices when working with Google Cloud resources
sources.evidence: If the permissions change outside of Terraform, Terraform on its next execution overwrites all permissions to represent the policy as defined in your configuration.

stem: A team creates an Infrastructure Manager deployment from a Terraform configuration that creates a VPC network, firewall rules, and Compute Engine VMs. The engineer who runs `gcloud infra-manager deployments apply` has the Infra Manager Admin role and the Service Account User role on the deployment's service account. The deployment fails with permission errors. The team must follow the principle of least privilege. Which two actions should the team take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Grant the Compute Admin role on the project to the engineer who runs the deployment command.
Grant the Infra Manager Agent role (`roles/config.agent`) to the service account that the deployment uses.
Create a key for the deployment's service account, and pass the key file to the deployment as an input value.
Grant the service account the Compute Network Admin, Compute Security Admin, and Compute Instance Admin (v1) roles.
Grant the Owner role on the project to the Infrastructure Manager service agent.

explanation: Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform with the identity of the service account that you name, not with the engineer's identity. That service account needs the Infra Manager Agent role for Infrastructure Manager's own work. It also needs permissions for every resource in the configuration. Compute Network Admin does not cover firewall rules, so the firewall rules also need Compute Security Admin.

whyWrong.A: The engineer's permissions do not create the resources. Infrastructure Manager executes Terraform as the service account.
whyWrong.C: Infrastructure Manager uses the service account identity directly. A key adds risk and is not a supported way to pass credentials.
whyWrong.E: Owner breaks least privilege. The service agent is not the identity that runs Terraform, so this grant does not fix the problem either.

sources.title: Configure the service account
sources.evidence: To work with Infra Manager, the service account needs the Infra Manager Agent (roles/config.agent) role.

sources.title: Configure the service account
sources.evidence: To create and manage Google Cloud resources that are defined in the Terraform configuration, the service account needs permissions specific to these resources.

stem: An operations team created a production VPC network and six firewall rules by hand. Company policy now requires that Terraform manages all network resources. Recreating the network would cause an outage. The change process requires that reviewers see every state change in the pull request before it happens. The team uses Terraform 1.9. What should the team do?

options.text: Run `terraform import` for each resource from an engineer's workstation, and then open a pull request with the resource blocks.
Delete the resources during a maintenance window, and let the pipeline recreate them from new Terraform resource blocks.
Add `import` blocks and matching resource blocks, and let the pipeline show the imports in `terraform plan` before `terraform apply`.
Download the state file, add the resources to it with a text editor, and upload the file to the state bucket.

explanation: Google prefers recreation, but here recreation causes an outage, so an approved import is correct. Since Terraform 1.5, an `import` block lets `terraform plan` preview the import and `terraform apply` run it. The pipeline shows the import in the pull request, which meets the review requirement. After the import, the team manages the resources only with Terraform.

whyWrong.A: The `terraform import` command writes to the state at once from a workstation. Reviewers do not see the change before it happens.
whyWrong.B: Recreation is Google's first choice only when it is practical. Here it causes a production outage.
whyWrong.D: Google says never to modify Terraform state manually, because corruption can cause major infrastructure problems.

sources.title: Import your Google Cloud resources into Terraform state
sources.evidence: Terraform version 1.5 lets you add an import block to your Terraform configuration. This allows import operations to be previewed during the plan operation and executed using the apply operation.

sources.title: Best practices for Terraform operations
sources.evidence: In cases where deleting old resources would create significant toil, use the terraform import command with explicit approval. After a resource is imported into Terraform, manage it exclusively with Terraform.

stem: A company runs all applications on GKE and manages Kubernetes manifests with a GitOps workflow. The platform team wants application teams to request Cloud SQL instances and Pub/Sub topics as Kubernetes resources in the same Git repositories. Changes made in the console must be reverted automatically, and policy violations must be blocked before resources are created. The platform team does not want to install or upgrade the controllers. What should the platform team use?

options.text: Infrastructure Manager with Cloud Build triggers that create a preview for each pull request and update the deployment on each merge.
The Config Connector add-on on a GKE Standard cluster, with a scheduled script that applies all manifests again every hour.
Terraform in Cloud Build with `gcloud beta terraform vet`, and a scheduled build that runs `terraform apply` every hour.
Config Controller, which hosts Config Connector together with Config Sync and Policy Controller.

explanation: Config Controller is a hosted version of Config Connector, so the platform team does not install or upgrade the controllers. Teams describe Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes resources in Git. Config Sync keeps the resources equal to the source of truth, so it reverts console changes. Policy Controller blocks policy violations before the resources are deployed.

whyWrong.A: Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform, not Kubernetes resources, and it corrects drift only when a new revision runs.
whyWrong.B: The platform team must install and upgrade the add-on itself, which it does not want. The add-on also gives no policy enforcement.
whyWrong.C: Terraform is not a Kubernetes-based workflow, an hourly apply leaves drift in place between runs, and `gcloud beta terraform vet` is Preview.

sources.title: Config Controller overview
sources.evidence: Config Controller is a hosted version of Config Connector that simplifies installation and maintenance. Config Controller also includes Policy Controller and Config Sync.

sources.title: Config Controller overview
sources.evidence: Automate drift detection and repair: Continuously monitor your infrastructure for drift from the defined state and enable automatic repairs.

sources.title: Infrastructure as Code on Google Cloud
sources.evidence: To manage Google Cloud resources through Kubernetes, use Config Controller and Config Connector.

stem: A bank deploys all infrastructure with Terraform from a Cloud Build pipeline. The security team wants to block any change that grants IAM roles to members outside the company domain before the change reaches production. The team also wants to find deployed resources that later drift into an insecure configuration. Which two actions should you recommend? (Choose two.)

options.text: Convert each saved plan to JSON, and run `gcloud beta terraform vet` with the organization's policy library before `terraform apply`.
Run `terraform validate` in the pipeline, and fail the build when the command reports an error.
After each apply, run automated security checks, such as Security Health Analytics, on the deployed resources.
Mark every Terraform output as sensitive, so that IAM members do not appear in the pipeline logs.
Turn on Object Versioning for the state bucket, so that the security team can compare state versions after each change.

explanation: Google recommends two controls. Before apply, a tool such as `gcloud beta terraform vet` checks the plan against policies, for example a constraint that allows only members from the company domain. The tool returns exit code 2 on a violation, which fails the build. After apply, continuous audits such as Security Health Analytics find infrastructure that drifts into an insecure state.

whyWrong.B: `terraform validate` checks syntax and structure only. It does not evaluate IAM members against a policy.
whyWrong.D: Sensitive outputs only hide values in output. They do not block a grant or detect insecure resources.
whyWrong.E: Versioning keeps old state for recovery. A manual comparison is not a policy check, and it misses changes made outside Terraform.

sources.title: Best practices for security
sources.evidence: When running Terraform in an automated pipeline, use a tool like gcloud terraform vet to check plan output against policies before it is applied. Doing so can detect security regressions before they happen.

sources.title: Best practices for security
sources.evidence: After the terraform apply command has executed, run automated security checks. These checks can help to ensure that infrastructure doesn't drift into an insecure state.

sources.title: Validate policies
sources.evidence: If violations are found, gcloud beta terraform vet returns exit code 2, and displays a list of violations.
